L4@P0: About the Introduction
L5@P0: 1.1 This Introduction explains the basic principles and structure of the Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC) system.
L6@P0: 1.2 The Introduction is intended to be used in conjunction with the Glossary and
L7@P0: the Manual. The Glossary defines terms used in the Introduction and elsewhere
L8@P0: in the Classification. The Manual offers advice on classifying in difficult areas,
L9@P0: and explains how to choose between related numbers.
L10@P0: Classification: What It Is and What It Does
L11@P0: 2.1	 Classification provides a system for organizing knowledge. Classification may
L12@P0: be used to organize knowledge represented in any form, e.g., books, documents,
L13@P0: electronic resources.
L14@P0: 2.2	 Notation is the system of symbols used to represent the classes in a classification system. In the Dewey Decimal Classification, the notation is expressed in
L15@P0: Arabic numerals. The notation gives both the unique meaning of the class and
L16@P0: its relation to other classes. The notation provides a universal language to identify the class and related classes, regardless of the fact that different words or
L17@P0: languages may be used to describe the class.
L18@P0: History, Current Use, and Development of the Dewey Decimal
L19@P0: Classification
L20@P0: 3.1 The Dewey Decimal Classification—conceived by Melvil Dewey in 1873 and
L21@P0: first published in 1876—is a general knowledge organization tool that is continuously revised to keep pace with knowledge. The system is further extended
L22@P0: through number building, interoperable translations, association with categorized content, and mappings to other subject schemes.
L23@P0: 3.2 The DDC is published in full and abridged editions by OCLC Online Computer
L24@P0: Library Center, Inc. The abridged edition is a logical truncation of the notational
L25@P0: and structural hierarchy of the corresponding full edition on which it is based,
L26@P0: and is intended for general collections of 20,000 titles or less. Both editions are
L27@P0: issued in print and electronic versions; the electronic versions are updated frequently and contain additional index entries and mapped vocabulary. OCLC
L28@P0: owns all copyright rights in the Dewey Decimal Classification, and licenses the
L29@P0: system for a variety of uses.
L30@P0: 3.3 The DDC is the most widely used classification system in the world. Libraries in more than 138 countries use the DDC to organize and provide access to
L31@P0-1: their collections, and DDC numbers are featured in the national bibliographies xxx
L32@P1: Dewey Decimal Classification
L33@P1: of more than sixty countries. Libraries of every type apply Dewey numbers on
L34@P1: a daily basis and share these numbers through a variety of means (including
L35@P1: WorldCat). Dewey is also used in a variety of applications on the web in support
L36@P1: of categorization, browsing, and retrieval.
L37@P1: 3.4 The DDC has been translated into over thirty languages. Since 1988, authorized
L38@P1: translations of the full and abridged editions of the DDC have been published or
L39@P1: are under way in Arabic, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Icelandic, Indonesian, Italian, Norwegian, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.
L40@P1: The DDC Summaries, the top three levels of the Dewey Decimal Classification
L41@P1: system, have been translated into Afrikaans, Arabic, Chinese, Czech, French,
L42@P1: German, Hebrew, Italian, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Scots Gaelic, Spanish, Swedish, and Vietnamese.
L43@P1: 3.5 One of Dewey’s great strengths is that the system is developed and maintained
L44@P1: in a national bibliographic agency, the Library of Congress. The Dewey editorial office is located in the Dewey Section of the Library of Congress, where
L45@P1: classification specialists annually assign over 60,000 DDC numbers to records
L46@P1: for works cataloged by the Library. Having the editorial office within the Dewey
L47@P1: Section enables the editors to detect trends in the literature that must be incorporated into the Classification. The editors prepare proposed schedule revisions
L48@P1: and expansions, and forward the proposals to the Decimal Classification Editorial Policy Committee (EPC) for review and recommended action.
L49@P1: 3.6 EPC is a ten-member international board whose main function is to advise the
L50@P1: editors and OCLC on matters relating to changes, innovations, and the general
L51@P1: development of the Classification. EPC represents the interests of DDC users;
L52@P1: its members come from national, public, school, and academic libraries, and
L53@P1: from library schools.
L54@P1: Overview of the Dewey Decimal Classification
L55@P1: Conceptual Framework
L56@P1: 4.1 The DDC is built on sound principles that make it ideal as a general knowledge organization tool: meaningful notation in universally recognized Arabic
L57@P1: numerals, well-defined categories, well-developed hierarchies, and a rich network of relationships among topics. In the DDC, basic classes are organized by
L58@P1: disciplines or fields of study. At the broadest level, the DDC is divided into ten
L59@P1: main classes, which together cover the entire world of knowledge. Each main
L60@P1: class is further divided into ten divisions, and each division into ten sections
L61@P1: (not all the numbers for the divisions and sections have been used).
L62@P1: 4.2 The main structure of the DDC is presented in the DDC Summaries preceding the schedules. The first summary contains the ten main classes. The second
L63@P1: summary contains the hundred divisions. The third summary contains the thousand sections. The headings associated with the numbers in the summaries have
L64@P1: been edited for browsing purposes, and do not necessarily match the complete
L65@P1-2: headings found in the schedules.xxxi
L66@P2: Introduction
L67@P2: 4.3 The ten main classes are:
L68@P2: 000 Computer science, information & general works
L69@P2: 100 Philosophy & psychology
L70@P2: 200 Religion
L71@P2: 300 Social sciences
L72@P2: 400 Language
L73@P2: 500 Science
L74@P2: 600 Technology
L75@P2: 700 Arts & recreation
L76@P2: 800 Literature
L77@P2: 900 History & geography
L78@P2: 4.4 Class 000 is the most general class, and is used for works not limited to any one
L79@P2: specific discipline, e.g., encyclopedias, newspapers, general periodicals. This
L80@P2: class is also used for certain specialized disciplines that deal with knowledge
L81@P2: and information, e.g., computer science, library and information science, journalism. Each of the other main classes (100–900) comprises a major discipline
L82@P2: or group of related disciplines.
L83@P2: 4.5 Class 100 covers philosophy, parapsychology and occultism, and psychology.
L84@P2: 4.6 Class 200 is devoted to religion.
L85@P2: 4.7 Class 300 covers the social sciences. Class 300 includes sociology, anthropology, statistics, political science, economics, law, public administration, social
L86@P2: problems and services, education, commerce, communications, transportation,
L87@P2: and customs.
L88@P2: 4.8 Class 400 comprises language, linguistics, and specific languages. Literature,
L89@P2: which is arranged by language, is found in 800.
L90@P2: 4.9 Class 500 is devoted to the natural sciences and mathematics.
L91@P2: 4.10 Class 600 is technology.
L92@P2: 4.11 Class 700 covers the arts: art in general, fine and decorative arts, music, and the
L93@P2: performing arts. Recreation, including sports and games, is also classed in 700.
L94@P2: 4.12 Class 800 covers literature, and includes rhetoric, prose, poetry, drama, etc.
L95@P2: Folk literature is classed with customs in 300.
L96@P2: 4.13 Class 900 is devoted primarily to history and geography. A history of a specific
L97@P2: subject is classed with the subject.
L98@P2: 4.14 Since the parts of the DDC are arranged by discipline, not subject, a subject
L99@P2: may appear in more than one class. For example, “clothing” has aspects that fall
L100@P2: under several disciplines. The psychological influence of clothing belongs in
L101@P2: 155.9 as part of the discipline of psychology; customs associated with clothing
L102@P2-3: belong in 391 as part of the discipline of customs; clothing in the sense of fashion design belongs in 746.9 as part of the discipline of the arts.xxxii
L103@P3: Dewey Decimal Classification
L104@P3: Notation
L105@P3: 4.15 Arabic numerals are used to represent each class in the DDC. The first digit in
L106@P3: each three-digit number represents the main class. For example, 500 represents
L107@P3: science. The second digit in each three-digit number indicates the division. For
L108@P3: example, 500 is used for general works on the sciences, 510 for mathematics,
L109@P3: 520 for astronomy, 530 for physics. The third digit in each three‑digit number
L110@P3: indicates the section. Thus, 530 is used for general works on physics, 531 for
L111@P3: classical mechanics, 532 for fluid mechanics, 533 for gas mechanics. The DDC
L112@P3: uses the convention that no number should have fewer than three digits; zeros
L113@P3: are used to fill out numbers.
L114@P3: 4.16 A decimal point, or dot, follows the third digit in a class number, after which
L115@P3: division by ten continues to the specific degree of classification needed. The dot
L116@P3: is not a decimal point in the mathematical sense, but a psychological pause to
L117@P3: break the monotony of numerical digits and to ease the transcription and copying of the class number. A number should never end in a 0 anywhere to the right
L118@P3: of the decimal point.
L119@P3: Principle of Hierarchy
L120@P3: 4.17	 Hierarchy in the DDC is expressed through structure and notation.
L121@P3: 4.18	 Structural hierarchy means that all topics (aside from the ten main classes) are
L122@P3: part of all the broader topics above them. The corollary is also true: whatever
L123@P3: is true of the whole is true of the parts. This important concept is called hierarchical force. Certain notes regarding the nature of a class hold true for all the
L124@P3: subordinate classes, including logically subordinate topics classed at coordinate numbers. (For a discussion of notes with hierarchical force, see paragraphs
L125@P3: 7.10–7.16 and 7.18–7.20.)
L126@P3: Because of the principle of hierarchical force, hierarchical notes are usually
L127@P3: given only once—at the highest level of application. For example, the scope
L128@P3: note at 700 applies to 730, to 737, and to 737.4. The words “Description, critical
L129@P3: appraisal . . .” found in the scope note at 700 also govern the critical appraisal of
L130@P3: coins in 737.4 Coins. In order to understand the structural hierarchy, the classifier must read up and down the schedules (and remember to turn the page).
L131@P3: 4.19	 Notational hierarchy is expressed by length of notation. Numbers at any given
L132@P3: level are usually subordinate to a class whose notation is one digit shorter; coordinate with a class whose notation has the same number of significant digits;
L133@P3: and superordinate to a class with numbers one or more digits longer. The underlined digits in the following example demonstrate this notational hierarchy:
L134@P3: 600 Technology (Applied sciences)
L135@P3: 630 Agriculture and related technologies
L136@P3: 636 Animal husbandry
L137@P3: 636.7 Dogs
L138@P3-4: 636.8 Catsxxxiii
L139@P4: Introduction
L140@P4: “Dogs” and “Cats” are more specific than (i.e., are subordinate to) “Animal husbandry”; they are equally specific as (i.e., are coordinate with) each other; and
L141@P4: “Animal husbandry” is less specific than (i.e., is superordinate to) “Dogs” and
L142@P4: “Cats.”
L143@P4: 4.20 Sometimes, other devices must be used to express hierarchy when it is not possible or desirable to do so through the notation. A see reference leads the classifier
L144@P4: to subdivisions of a subject located outside the notational hierarchy. A centered
L145@P4: entry (so called because its numbers, heading, and notes appear in the center of
L146@P4: the page) constitutes a major departure from notational hierarchy. A centered
L147@P4: entry is used to indicate and relate structurally a span of numbers that together
L148@P4: form a single concept for which there is no specific hierarchical notation available. In the DDC, centered entries are always flagged typographically by the
L149@P4: symbol > in the number column.
L150@P4: Classifying with the DDC
L151@P4: 5.1 Classifying a work with the DDC requires determining the subject, the disciplinary focus, and, if applicable, the approach or form. (For a discussion of
L152@P4: approach or form, see paragraph 8.3.)
L153@P4: Determining the Subject of a Work
L154@P4: 5.2 Classifying a work properly depends first upon determining the subject of the
L155@P4: work in hand. A key element in determining the subject is the author’s intent.
L156@P4: (A) The title is often a clue to the subject, but should never be the sole source
L157@P4: of analysis. For example, Opera could be the title of a work on the familiar dramatic musical art form or on the web browser Opera. Likewise,
L158@P4: a title with specific terms that are subdivisions of a field may in fact
L159@P4: use such terms symbolically to represent the broader topic. For example, titles containing terms like chromosomes, DNA, double helix, genes,
L160@P4: and genomes may use these terms symbolically to represent the whole
L161@P4: subject of biochemical genetics.
L162@P4: (B) The table of contents may list the main topics discussed. Chapter headings may substitute for the absence of a table of contents. Chapter subheadings often prove useful.
L163@P4: (C) The preface or introduction usually states the author‘s purpose. If a foreword is provided, it often indicates the subject of the work and suggests
L164@P4: the place of the work in the development of thought on the subject. The
L165@P4: book jacket or accompanying material may include a summary of the
L166@P4: subject content.
L167@P4: (D) A scan of the text itself may provide further guidance or confirm preliminary subject analysis.
L168@P4-5: (E) Bibliographical references and index entries are sources of subject information.xxxiv
L169@P5: Dewey Decimal Classification
L170@P5:  (F) Cataloging copy from centralized cataloging services is often helpful by
L171@P5: providing subject headings, classification numbers, and notes. Such copy
L172@P5: appears in online services, and on the verso of the title page of many
L173@P5: books as part of Cataloging‑in‑Publication (CIP) data. Data from these
L174@P5: sources should be verified with the book in hand, since the cataloging
L175@P5: record is based on prepublication information.
L176@P5: (G) Occasionally, consultation of outside sources such as reviews, reference
L177@P5: works, and subject experts may be required to determine the subject of
L178@P5: the work.
L179@P5: Determining the Discipline of a Work
L180@P5: 5.3 After determining the subject, the classifier must then select the proper discipline, or field of study, of the work.
L181@P5: 5.4 The guiding principle of the DDC is that a work is classed in the discipline for
L182@P5: which it is intended, rather than the discipline from which the work derives.
L183@P5: This enables works that are used together to be found together. For example, a
L184@P5: general work by a zoologist on agricultural pest control should be classed in
L185@P5: agriculture, not zoology, along with other works on agricultural pest control.
L186@P5: 5.5 Once the subject has been determined, and information on the discipline has
L187@P5: been found, the classifier will turn to the schedules. The summaries are a good
L188@P5: means of mental navigation. The headings and notes in the schedules themselves and the Manual provide much guidance. The Relative Index may help by
L189@P5: suggesting the disciplines in which a subject is normally treated. (For a discussion of the summaries, see paragraph 7.1; for a discussion of the Manual, see
L190@P5: paragraphs 10.1–10.6; for a discussion of the Relative Index, see paragraphs
L191@P5: 11.1–11.15.)
L192@P5: 5.6 If the Relative Index is used, the classifier must still rely on the structure of the
L193@P5: Classification and various aids throughout to arrive at the proper place to classify a work. Even the most promising Relative Index citations must be verified
L194@P5: in the schedules; the schedules are the only place where all the information
L195@P5: about coverage and use of the numbers may be found.
L196@P5: More Than One Subject in the Same Discipline
L197@P5: 5.7 A work may include multiple subjects treated separately or in relation to one
L198@P5: another from the viewpoint of a single discipline. Use the following guidelines
L199@P5: in determining the best placement for the work:
L200@P5: (A) Class a work dealing with interrelated subjects with the subject that is
L201@P5: being acted upon. This is called the rule of application, and takes precedence over any other rule. For instance, class an analytical work dealing with Shakespeare’s influence on Keats with Keats. Similarly, class a
L202@P5: work on the influence of the Great Depression on 20th century American
L203@P5: art with American art.
L204@P5-6: (B) Class a work on two subjects with the subject receiving fuller treatment.xxxv
L205@P6: Introduction
L206@P6: (C) If two subjects receive equal treatment, and are not used to introduce
L207@P6: or explain one another, class the work with the subject whose number
L208@P6: comes first in the DDC schedules. This is called the first‑of‑two rule. For
L209@P6: example, a history dealing equally with the United States and Japan, in
L210@P6: which the United States is discussed first and is given first in the title, is
L211@P6: classed with the history of Japan because 952 Japan precedes 973 United
L212@P6: States.
L213@P6: Sometimes, specific instructions are given to use numbers that do not
L214@P6: come first in the schedules. For example, at 598, the note “class comprehensive works on warm-blooded vertebrates in 599” tells the classifier to
L215@P6: ignore the first-of-two rule and class a work on birds (598) and mammals
L216@P6: (599) in 599, which is the comprehensive number for warm‑blooded vertebrates.
L217@P6: Also disregard the first‑of‑two rule when the two topics are the two
L218@P6: major subdivisions of a subject. For example, primary forms of energy
L219@P6: (333.792) and secondary forms of energy (333.793) taken together constitute most of 333.79 Energy. Works covering both of these topics are
L220@P6: classed in 333.79 (not 333.792).
L221@P6: (For a discussion of comprehensive numbers, see paragraphs 7.16 and
L222@P6: 7.18–7.19.)
L223@P6: (D) Class a work on three or more subjects that are all subdivisions of a
L224@P6: broader subject in the first higher number that includes them all (unless
L225@P6: one subject is treated more fully than the others). This is called the rule
L226@P6: of three. For example, a history of Portugal (946.9), Sweden (948.5), and
L227@P6: Greece (949.5) is classed with the history of Europe (940).
L228@P6: (E) Subdivisions beginning with zero should be avoided if there is a choice
L229@P6: between 0 and 1–9 at the same point in the hierarchy of the notation.
L230@P6: Similarly, subdivisions beginning with 00 should be avoided when there
L231@P6: is a choice between 00 and 0. This is called the rule of zero.
L232@P6: More Than One Discipline
L233@P6: 5.8 Treating a subject from the point of view of more than one discipline is different
L234@P6: from treating several subjects in one discipline. Use the following guidelines in
L235@P6: determining the best placement for the work:
L236@P6: (A) Use the interdisciplinary number provided in the schedules or Relative
L237@P6: Index if one is given. An important consideration in using such an interdisciplinary number is that the work must contain significant material
L238@P6: on the discipline in which the interdisciplinary number is found. For
L239@P6: example, 305.231 (a sociology number) is provided for interdisciplinary
L240@P6: works on child development. However, if a work that is interdisciplinary
L241@P6: with respect to child development gives little emphasis to social development and a great deal of emphasis to the psychological and physical
L242@P6: development of the child (155.4 and 612.6, respectively), class it in 155.4
L243@P6-7: (the first number in the schedules of the next two obvious choices). In xxxvi
L244@P7: Dewey Decimal Classification
L245@P7: short, interdisciplinary numbers are not absolute; they are to be used
L246@P7: only when applicable. (For a discussion of interdisciplinary numbers, see
L247@P7: paragraphs 7.16, 7.18–7.19, and 11.8–11.9.)
L248@P7: (B) Class works not given an interdisciplinary number in the discipline
L249@P7: given the fullest treatment in the work. For example, a work dealing with
L250@P7: both the scientific and the engineering principles of electrodynamics
L251@P7: is classed in 537.6 if the engineering aspects are introduced primarily
L252@P7: for illustrative purposes, but in 621.31 if the basic scientific theories are
L253@P7: only preliminary to the author’s exposition of engineering principles and
L254@P7: practices.
L255@P7: (C) When classifying interdisciplinary works, do not overlook the possibilities of main class 000 Computer science, information & general works,
L256@P7: e.g., 080 for a collection of interviews of famous people from various
L257@P7: disciplines.
L258@P7: Any other situation is treated in the same fashion as those found in the instructions at More Than One Subject in the Same Discipline (paragraph 5.7).

L291@P8: Key Features of the Schedules and Tables
L292@P8: Summaries
L293@P8: 7.1 	 Summaries provide an overview of the structure of classes. Two types of summaries appear in the DDC:
L294@P8: (A) DDC Summaries, the summaries of the top three levels of the DDC, are
L295@P8: found in front of the schedules in volume 2. (For a discussion of DDC
L296@P8: Summaries, see paragraphs 4.2–4.13.)
L297@P8: (B) Single‑level summaries in the schedules and tables provide an overview
L298@P8: of classes with subdivisions that cover more than three pages. For example, 380 Commerce, communications, transportation has the following
L299@P8: summary:
L300@P8: SUMMARY
L301@P8: 381 Commerce (Trade)
L302@P8: 382 International commerce (Foreign trade)
L303@P8: 383 Postal communication
L304@P8: 384 Communications
L305@P8: 385 Railroad transportation
L306@P8: 386 Inland waterway and ferry transportation
L307@P8: 387 Water, air, space transportation
L308@P8: 388 Transportation
L309@P8: 389 Metrology and standardization
L310@P8: Entries
L311@P8: 7.2 Entries in the schedules and tables are composed of a DDC number in the number column (the column at the left margin), a heading describing the class that
L312@P8: the number represents, and often one or more notes. DDC numbers are listed
L313@P8: in groups of three digits for ease of reading and copying. All entries (numbers,
L314@P8: headings, and notes) should be read in the context of the hierarchy. (For a discussion of the principle of hierarchy, see paragraphs 4.17–4.20.)
L315@P8: 7.3 The first three digits of schedule numbers (main classes, divisions, sections)
L316@P8-9: appear only once in the number column, when first used. They are repeated at xxxviii
L317@P9: Dewey Decimal Classification
L318@P9: the top of each page where their subdivisions continue. Subordinate numbers
L319@P9: appear in the number column, beginning with a decimal point, with the initial
L320@P9: three digits understood.
L321@P9: 7.4 Table numbers are given in full in the number column of the tables, and are
L322@P9: never used alone. There are four numbered tables in Abridged Edition 15:
L323@P9: T1 Standard Subdivisions
L324@P9: T2 Geographic Areas, and Biography
L325@P9: T3 Subdivisions for Individual Literatures, for Specific Literary Forms
L326@P9: T4 Subdivisions of Individual Languages and Language Families
L327@P9: Except for notation from Table 1 (which may be added to any number unless
L328@P9: there is an instruction in the schedules or tables to the contrary), table notation
L329@P9: may be added only as instructed in the schedules and tables. (For a detailed discussion of the use of the four tables, see paragraphs 8.3–8.16.)
L330@P9: 7.5 Some numbers in the schedules and tables are enclosed in parentheses or square
L331@P9: brackets. Numbers and notes in parentheses provide options to standard practice. Numbers in square brackets represent topics that have been relocated or
L332@P9: discontinued, or are unassigned. Square brackets are also used for standard subdivision concepts that are represented in another location. Bracketed numbers
L333@P9: should never be used. (For a discussion of options, see paragraphs 12.1–12.7; for
L334@P9: a discussion of relocations and discontinuations, see paragraphs 7.22–7.23; for a

L1@P0-1: Library of Congress Classification: Module 1.1In this introductory module, we will provide a very brief history and overview of the
L2@P1: Library of Congress’ classification system, which at times during this training may be
L3@P1: referred to as Library of Congress Classification, LC Classification, or even LCC.
L4@P1: We will then describe the system at a high level, and conclude with some definitions of
L5@P1: terms that will be used throughout the training.
L6@P1: 2
L7@P1-2: Library of Congress Classification: Module 1.1Development of LC classification began in 1897, when it was determined that the existing
L8@P2: classification system – which was based on Thomas Jefferson’s system of organization,
L9@P2: which in turn was based on 17th and 18th century philosophical thought – was insufficient
L10@P2: for the growing collection. The Library needed a system that was more granular and that
L11@P2: could be updated regularly. The Librarian of Congress asked James Hanson, Head of the
L12@P2: Catalogue Division, and Charles Martel, the Chief Classifier, to find a solution to the
L13@P2: problem. After much exploration, they decided to create a new classification system for LC.
L14@P2: Four years after the decision was made to develop a wholly new system, the first schedules,
L15@P2: E through F, the history of the Americas, were published.
L16@P2: Schedules were published as they were ready. Today, there are 21 main classes and over 225
L17@P2: subclasses, with more subclasses under development in the discipline of law. There are over
L18@P2: 400,000 individually established classification numbers.
L19@P2: 3
L20@P2-3: Library of Congress Classification: Module 1.1LCC is continually updated; in fact, dozens of new numbers are added to the schedules
L21@P3: every month. Until 2014, new editions of the schedules were published irregularly. A new
L22@P3: edition might be prompted by a major development or reorganization of a particular
L23@P3: schedule, say, the schedule for Islam. More typically, a new edition was published when the
L24@P3: remaining stock of the existing edition was sold out.
L25@P3: Now, all of the schedules are available as free PDFs on LC’s website, and new editions are
L26@P3: generally published annually.
L27@P3: 4
L28@P3-4: Library of Congress Classification: Module 1.1Today, the most up-to-date information about approved classification numbers can be found
L29@P4: in Classification Web, LC’s online subscription service.
L30@P4: Class Web is updated daily and it is the best method for assuring that you are using the most
L31@P4: up-to-date classification numbers in your cataloging.
L32@P4: As we mentioned, there are also free PDFs available on LC’s website. Some of the
L33@P4: schedules are also available through LC’s Linked Data Service, from which they can be
L34@P4: downloaded in a variety of formats. Additional schedules will be added to the Linked Data
L35@P4: Service in the future.
L36@P4: You might be wondering, if the schedules are available for free in PDF, then why is there
L37@P4: also a subscription-based version? Why would some pay for it, if it’s available for free? It is
L38@P4: because Classification Web provides additional functionality. There are several searching
L39@P4: options built into the system that make navigating the classification schedules easier and
L40@P4: more efficient. We will demonstrate those searching techniques in a later module.

L56@P6: Not all of the valid numbers are printed, though. Personal, corporate, and geographic names,
L57@P6: and titles, are not generally printed, unless tradition or policy dictates otherwise for a
L58@P6: specific schedule. For example, by tradition all classification numbers for individual
L59@P6: philosophers are printed, but classification numbers for individual artists are not. Numbers

L67@P6-7: Library of Congress Classification: Module 1.1LCC uses alphanumeric notation. Each classification number begins with one or more
L68@P7: letters, which is followed by a number that may be a whole number or a whole number with
L69@P7: a decimal, such as 2301, 111, 756.5, as shown in the call numbers on the screen. Additional
L70@P7: letters and numbers are added in a defined order to create a predictable arrangement on the
L71@P7: shelves.
L72@P7: Some of those letter-number combinations are called cutter numbers. In the examples on
L73@P7: your screen, the cutters are .T5, .A23, .N6, and M45.
L74@P7: A cutter number is a tool for providing logical sub-arrangement under a classification
L75@P7: number. It is a method of representing words or names with a letter of the alphabet and one
L76@P7: or more Arabic numerals. Some cutters are preceded by a decimal point.

L94@P10: in the early 20th century, and the structure of LCC sometimes reflects an understanding of

L46: ## Principle of Organization
L47: The organization of knowledge in UDC is discipline-based. This means that concepts are subsumed and placed in the field under which they are studied. This particular feature is usually implemented in UDC by re-using the same concept in various combinations with the main subject, e.g. a code for language in common auxiliaries of language is used to derive numbers for ethnic grouping, individual languages in linguistics and individual literatures. Or, a code from the auxiliaries of place, e.g.
L48: (410) United Kingdom, uniquely representing the concept of United Kingdom can be used to express 911(410) Regional geography of United Kingdom and 94(410) History of United Kingdom.
L49: ## UDC Hierarchic Structure
L50: UDC's most innovative and influential feature is its ability to express not just simple subjects but relations between subjects. This facility is added to a hierarchic structure, in which knowledge is divided into ten classes, then each class is subdivided into its logical parts, each subdivision is further subdivided, and so on. The more detailed the subdivision, the longer the number that represents it. This is made possible by the decimal notation (see cite5†UDC notational system ).

L85: Each main UDC class may also contain tables called special auxiliaries (or special auxiliary numbers), which express aspects that are recurrent, but in a limited subject range. These are usually facets of concepts related to operations, techniques, processes, materials, agents etc. They are listed only in particular sections of the main tables. Special auxiliary numbers can be recognized as they all begin with one of these three specific symbols/indicators: .0 (point nought), - (hyphen) or ' (apostrophe).
L86: Any UDC number beginning with any of these symbols can be combined with any other UDC number in its designated area of application.
L87: ### 2. Common auxiliary tables
L88: 
L89: These tables contain common auxiliary signs and common auxiliary numbers.
L90: #### 2.1 Common Auxiliary Signs
L91: 
L92: The signs (e.g. the plus, the stroke, the colon) are used to link two (or more) numbers, so expressing relations of various kinds between two (or more) subjects.
L93: Notation  | Description
L94: --- | ---
L95: +  | Coordination. Addition (plus sign). Table 1a
L96: /  | Consecutive extension (oblique stroke sign). Table 1a
L97: :  | Simple relation (colon sign). Table 1b
L98: ::  | Order-fixing (double colon sign). Table 1b
L99: []  | Subgrouping (square brackets). Table 1b
L100: *  | Introduces non-UDC notation (asterisk). Table 1h
L101: A/Z  | Direct alphabetical specification. Table 1h
L102:

L104: #### 2.2 Common Auxiliary Numbers
L105: 
L106: These are tables enumerating concepts that denote recurrent characteristics, applicable over a range of subjects; the auxiliary is simply added at the end of the number for the subject. Common auxiliaries, are applicable throughout the main tables, and represent notions such as place, language of the text and physical form of the document, which may occur in almost any subject.
L107: Notation  | Description

L109: =...  | Common auxiliaries of language. Table 1c

L113: "..."  | Common auxiliaries of time. Table 1g helps to make minute division of time e.g.: "1993-1996"

L120: ## UDC Synthetic Structure
L121: UDC is an analytico-synthetic and/or faceted classification. It allows an unlimited combination of attributes of a subject and relationships between subjects to be expressed. UDC codes from different tables can be combined to present various aspects of document content and form, e.g. 94(410)"19"(075) History (main subject) of United Kingdom (place) in 20th century (time), a textbook (document form). Or: 37:2 Relationship between Education and Religion.
L122: Complex UDC expressions can be accurately parsed into constituent elements.
L123: Example:
L124: 
L125: Tourist maps of Grafton County (USA, Maine) from 1970s as a pdf file will be expressed as a combination of simple UDC numbers as follows:

L127: 338.48(734.211.4)"197"(084.3)(0.034.2PDF)
L128:

L131: 338.48 Tourism
L132: (734.211.4) auxiliary number of place: Grafton County [USA, Maine]
L133: "197" time auxiliary number for 1970s
L134: (084.3) auxiliary number of form - map

L46: In 1885, cite38†Paul Otlet†en.wikipedia.org , a young Belgian barrister already noted for his work in documentation and his collaborator cite39†Henry La Fontaine†en.wikipedia.org were working on the projected Universal Bibliographic Repertory, which was intended to become a comprehensive classified index to all published information.
L47: A means of arranging the entries would be needed, and Otlet, having heard of Dewey’s Decimal Classification wrote to Melvil Dewey in 1895 and obtained permission to translate it into French.
L48: ## The first analytico-synthetic classification
L49: Otlet and La Fontaine saw in Decimal Classification a taxonomy of human knowledge that could be expressed (as they said in a conference paper) ‘in an international language - that of numbers’; they saw too that, because of the extensibility of decimal numbers, it could readily accommodate the detail needed for bibliographic rather than strictly library use.
L50: The idea outgrew the plan of mere translation, and a number of radical innovations were made, adapting the purely enumerative classification (in which all the subjects envisaged are already listed and coded) into one which allows for synthesis (that is, the construction of compound numbers to denote interrelated subjects that could never be exhaustively foreseen); various possible relations between subjects were identified, and symbols assigned to represent them.
L51: They also realized that characteristics common to many subjects could be assembled as a separate list; repeated patterns of digits where the same characteristic of division was applied were already present to some extent in Dewey’s first edition, but now the further step was taken of detaching the terminal digits and listing them as tables of auxiliary numbers, which could be added as required by the user.
L52: This synthetic principle meant that a level of detail could be obtained much greater than what was actually displayed in the published scheme: higher precision combined with economy of presentation. At the same time, Otlet and La Fontaine were expanding the purely enumerative content, to provide for the extensive requirements of the Repertory, and the result was a scheme both more copious and more sophisticated than its predecessor.
L53: cite40†Image: UDC 1900 and 1902 editions It contained about 33,000 subdivisions. It was published by the KB, in French, from 1902 to 1907, and was called the 'Handbook to the Universal Bibliographic Repertory' (Manuel du Répertoire Bibliographique Universel). It was in fact the first edition of UDC.
L54: ## UDC expansion
L55: The scheme continued to expand, though interrupted by the First World War, and work progressed on a second edition, in which editorship was shared with Frits Donker Duyvis of the Dutch Patent Office, who was responsible for the extensive revision and expansion of the science and technology sections. It was published from 1927 to 1933, and by now had over 70,000 subdivisions.
L56: The Universal Bibliographic Repertory, the impetus for the scheme, was proving unmanageable, and this edition was now offered independently under the title 'Classification Decimale Universelle', the name by which (in various translations) it is still known.
L57: This edition became the master version of UDC, and remained so until 1993, when a new database became the authoritative source; from 1933 to 1993 the second French edition, as modified and augmented by approved amendments collected in various supplements and later in the serial Extensions and Corrections to the UDC, was the official source for all UDC editions.
L58: A third edition, the first in German, was next begun, under the editorship of Carl Walther, and published from 1934 to 1951; this was probably double the size of the second, about 140,000 subdivisions.
L59: ## Change of UDC ownership
L60: The Institut International de Bibliographic (IIB) in 1931 became the Institut International de Documentation (IID), now with its headquarters at the Hague; in 1937 it changed to the Federation Internationale de Documentation (FID), and in 1988 changed again to the International Federation for Information and Documentation (FID), its name until the federation's dissolution in 2000. FID remained for many years the centre for the management and maintenance of UDC, and played a central role.
L61: In 1991, acting on the recommendations of the specially formed Task Force for UDC System Development, it held talks with several UDC publishers about restructuring the finance, management and maintenance of the scheme to ensure its future into the next century. As a result of these talks, the UDC Consortium (UDCC) was formed, with FID, BSI and four other publishers as founder members. All rights were transferred to the UDCC on 1 January 1992.
L62: Its first priority was the creation of a database of 60,000 entries, known as the Master Reference File (MRF), which was completed in the spring of 1993 and is now the authoritative statement of the content of UDC. The full editions (totalling about 220,000 entries) remain valid, and, as resources permit, extended sets of some classes to full edition level may be entered in the database.
L63: Since August 1949, authorized amendments have appeared in Extensions and Corrections to the UDC, issued at first six-monthly, later annually.
L64: The working languages of FID were English, French and German, and these remained the medium for the maintenance and management of UDC (including all amendments appearing in Extensions and Corrections to the UDC) until 1992, when the UDCC took over. The official language of the Consortium is English.
L65: Since the early editions, UDC has been translated into many other languages and is used in over hundred countries worldwide (c.f. "Bibliographical survey of UDC Editions", FID Publication 573. L120: ## UDC Synthetic Structure
L121: UDC is an analytico-synthetic and/or faceted classification. It allows an unlimited combination of attributes of a subject and relationships between subjects to be expressed. UDC codes from different tables can be combined to present various aspects of document content and form, e.g. 94(410)"19"(075) History (main subject) of United Kingdom (place) in 20th century (time), a textbook (document form). Or: 37:2 Relationship between Education and Religion.

L127: 338.48(734.211.4)"197"(084.3)(0.034.2PDF)

L133: "197" time auxiliary number for 1970s
